wiring.title: Cart wiring, in plain words
steps: Battery (12.8 V LiFePO4) → 30 A fuse → switch → a fuse block with three rails (arm, cart motors, Pi). See the power plan below.

From the block: The cart-motor rail (10 A fuse) goes to the four DRV8871 boards and the TB6612FNG's motor-power pin (the jaws are run at half PWM, about 6 V), the arm rail (10 A fuse, then a 12 V step-down converter) goes to the arm's Waveshare bus servo adapter (it talks to the Pi over USB, so the arm stays on its own USB link and needs no extra wiring), and the Pi rail (3 A fuse) goes to the 12 V → 5 V converter that powers the Pi.

The Pi (a Pi 3 now, a Pi 5 later; the wiring is the same) talks to the PCA9685 over I2C: just 4 wires (3.3 V, ground, SDA, SCL). The PCA9685 then sends two PWM signals to each driver board: one for forward, one for reverse. The jaw TB6612FNG gets its speed from the PCA9685 and its direction from 4 Pi GPIO pins.

Each driver's output goes straight to its motor. Each motor's encoder has 4 wires (power, ground, channel A, channel B): the two channel wires go to Pi GPIO pins, 12 pins in total. If the encoders are 5 V, put the channels through a level shifter first, or power the encoders from the Pi's 3.3 V.
Join all the grounds (battery, drivers, PCA9685, Pi) at one point. Keep thick motor wires away from thin signal wires.
Before the first power-up, with no motors plugged in, check the 5 V and 3.3 V rails with a meter. Then plug in one motor at a time at a low PWM.

items.item: STS3215 servos, 12 V 30 kg version (C018 / Waveshare ST3215 30 kg)
items.note: Follower arm only (no leader). Rule: buy on Amazon UK if servos + board come under about £135; otherwise ArmDojo (Singapore, about S$30 each, free shipping over S$110, ~20% UK VAT on delivery): https://armdojo.com/products/feetech-sts3215-serial-bus-servo. Not stocked by RobotShop UK (twice the price, out of stock), The Pi Hut, Pimoroni, RS or Farnell. Each servo comes with a 15 cm cable. Arrived.

items.item: SO-101 robot arm: 3D-printed parts
items.note: These parts are 3D-printed, not bought: download the STL files and print them in PLA. Design repo: https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100

items.item: Servo driver board (Waveshare Bus Servo Adapter A)
items.note: One board drives all six servos, daisy-chained. No Arduino needed: the laptop runs the software over USB. Also on Amazon UK and ArmDojo (https://armdojo.com/products/waveshare-bus-servo-adapter-board); buy from the same shop as the servos.

items.item: Spare servo cables (3-pin 5264)
items.note: Optional, for longer joint runs. Ready-made connectors.

items.item: USB cable
items.note: Match the driver board's USB-C port.

items.item: 12 V power supply, at least 5 A (100–240 V input)
items.note: This replaces a battery for the arm in the UK: the bench supply runs all six servos through the Waveshare adapter. Check home first: label must say 12 V and 5 A or more, 5.5 × 2.1 mm barrel plug, centre-positive. Otherwise buy on Amazon. 100–240 V input so it works in Brazil.

items.item: PLA filament, 1 kg spool
items.note: Follower arm needs about 400 g. Weigh the current spool first (subtract about 230 g for an empty plastic spool). Print one test part before the rest.

items.item: Raspberry Pi 3 power supply, 5.1 V 2.5 A micro-USB (UK plug)
items.note: Powers the Pi 3 on the bench in the UK, so no battery or converter is needed. Skip it if you already have a good phone charger that says 5 V and 2.5 A or more. Cheap chargers sag and make the Pi reboot.

items.item: Travel plug adapter, UK to Brazil (type N, takes UK plugs)
items.note: So the 12 V bench supply and the Pi charger (both take 100–240 V) plug into the wall in São Paulo. About 30 g.

items.item: Bambu Lab A1 printer (no AMS)
items.note: GTMax3D is an authorised Bambu Lab reseller in Brazil. Other shops: bambulab.com/pt-br/where-to-buy. Pending a chat with Mum.

items.item: Neodymium disc magnets 10 x 3 mm, N52 (collar closure)
items.note: 4 per collar, 2 glued into each closure tab with opposite poles facing (see cad/pipe_collar.py). Buy a pack of 20 or more from a UK magnet shop (First4Magnets, Amazon UK, eBay UK): about £0.30-0.50 each, about £7-9 for 20. The price is an estimate and no listing has been checked yet. Use epoxy or cyanoacrylate; keep them away from the servos and the Pi SD card. Quantity scales with the number of collars (one per pod hole).

items.item: PLA/PETG filament
Pipe, tank and plywood
items.note: Bulky and generic, so buy locally.

items.item: Cart drive and roll motors: 12 V worm-gear motor, 28 mm, with Hall encoder, about 60 rpm
items.for: Cart: 2 pipe drives + 2 roll drives (the roll motor turns the whole cart round the pipe)
items.note: Cheapest reliable: the 28 mm 'GA28' / 'JGY-28' style self-locking worm motor with a 2-channel Hall encoder. Pick the 12 V, 50–65 rpm version whose listing shows 3 kg·cm or more rated torque and says 'encoder'. Link is a search because AliExpress listings come and go; check the seller has 500+ sales and 4.7+ stars. Shipping about 2–4 weeks standard (about 10 days with Choice). UK import VAT is added at checkout. Backup if you want it in a week: a similar 12 V worm motor with encoder on eBay UK, about £15 each. Prices are estimates, not quotes. ORDER ONE NOW for the bench test (hold on a tilted pipe, exact size for the CAD); the other three follow once it checks out. The old hinge worm drives are gone in the new design: the four motors now drive an omni wheel each (a drive wheel and a roll wheel on each hand). Later production units are built in Brazil, so keep the listing's model name and size: the same family has to be easy to find on Mercado Livre. DIMENSIONS: real motors of this type are about 28 mm wide but often 60–75 mm long once the worm box and the encoder cap are counted, against the 55 mm in the CAD; and the worm gearbox puts the output shaft at a right angle to the motor, while the CAD has the motor in line with the worm shaft. Measure the real one and update MOTOR_L and the brackets before cutting anything. The roll motor can stall while holding a load: measure the stall current (the DRV8871 takes 3.6 A peak).

items.item: Reference omni wheels (bench test only): bought 38 mm double aluminium omni wheel
items.for: Bench test (task 290): compare the printed wheel against a bought pair
items.note: Only a reference pair, not for the cart: the cart uses the printed wheels below. Price about £18.89 each on Amazon UK, an estimate.

items.item: Shaft hub for omni wheel: 6 mm D-shaft to wheel bore
items.note: Check which shaft the motor listing has (6 mm D-shaft assumed) and the bore of the wheel you buy; some omni wheels ship with a hub. Buy to match both.

items.item: Stainless steel balls (304/316), 10–12 mm, for the printed ball cups
items.for: Cart: passive ball rollers (8 on the cart, 4 per hand); extras for the bench test
items.note: Stainless, not chrome steel, which rusts outdoors. Bought for the bench test against the Delrin balls (a couple of sizes if cheap); the final line becomes 8 balls of the winner plus spares. The cups are 3D-printed in PETG or nylon: no purchase. Standard stock item, to confirm for Brazil.

items.item: Delrin (acetal) balls, 10–12 mm, for the printed ball cups
items.for: Cart: passive ball rollers; extras for the bench test
items.note: Bought for the bench test against the stainless balls (sticking, drag, rust, water held in the cup). Same size range. Standard stock item, to confirm for Brazil.

items.item: Magnet tape, flexible, adhesive (home ring round the pipe)
items.for: Track: home station near the base of the track
items.note: A ring of tape all the way round the pipe means 'you are at home'; a single point magnet shortly after it marks zero (zero roll angle and zero position). The 10 x 3 mm N52 disc magnets already in this list can serve as the point magnets, plus a few more as optional checkpoints at corners and legs. Check the tape's polarity and strength against the sensor below.

items.item: Hall sensor board (3.3 V)
items.for: Cart: reads the home ring and the zero magnet (one per hand, one spare)
items.note: The controller counts wheel turns for roll angle and position and corrects drift at the home station. If the cart is lost it drives until it hits the ring, moves on to the point magnet and rolls until it finds it.

items.item: Optional: BNO055 IMU board
items.for: Cart: absolute roll angle on horizontal pipe sections (optional)
items.note: Only if counting wheel turns plus the home magnets is not accurate enough. Not needed for the first bench test.

items.item: Jaw motor: N20 worm-gear micro motor with encoder, 6 V, about 30 rpm
items.note: Assumed: the jaw only has to swing 92 degrees against a light grip, so about 0.1–0.2 N·m at the pin is enough; a 6 V N20 worm motor with encoder gives roughly that at 20–40 rpm, and a worm box locks the jaw shut with the power off. Run it at 6 V by capping the PWM at 50% from the 12 V rail. If it turns out too weak, step up to a 12 V N20 at 100 rpm with an extra gear. Shipping 2–4 weeks. DIMENSIONS: an N20 is 12 × 10 mm and about 25 mm long plus gearbox, smaller than the 16 × 30 mm motor + 12 mm box in the CAD (cart_sleeves.py), so it fits, but the right-angle shaft and the keyed pin mount need redrawing. Also check it really has an encoder; many N20 listings sell it as an add-on.

items.item: Motor driver: DRV8871 single H-bridge board (3.6 A peak, 6.5–45 V)
items.note: Swapped in for the TB6612FNG on the four 12 V motors. The TB6612FNG is only rated 1.2 A continuous (3.2 A for a moment) per channel, and a 28 mm worm motor stalled at 12 V can pull 1.5–3 A, so it is under-rated for these. The DRV8871 takes 3.6 A peak, has a current-limit resistor, and needs just two PWM inputs, which the PCA9685 can supply. Also on Amazon UK as 'DRV8871 motor driver' for about £6 each, delivered in 1–2 days: https://www.amazon.co.uk/s?k=DRV8871+motor+driver. Check the real stall current on the motor you receive.

items.item: Motor driver: TB6612FNG dual H-bridge board
items.note: One board runs both jaw motors (about 0.5 A each, well inside its 1.2 A). Pimoroni is the safe UK source (real Pololu-style board, a few pounds more). A generic one from AliExpress is about £2: https://www.aliexpress.com/wholesale?SearchText=TB6612FNG. Only 1 board is needed, not 3, because the big motors use the DRV8871.

items.item: PCA9685 16-channel I2C PWM board
items.note: Gives 16 PWM outputs over two Pi wires (I2C). Six motors need 12 (two per motor), so 4 are spare. A generic board is about £6 on Amazon UK or OnBuy (search 'PCA9685 16 channel'): https://www.amazon.co.uk/s?k=PCA9685+16+channel. Priced here at the cheap one.

items.item: Level shifter, 4-channel 3.3 V / 5 V (bi-directional)
items.note: Needed only if the encoders run on 5 V, as most do: the Pi pins die above 3.3 V. Better: power the encoders from the Pi's 3.3 V pin, which most 5 V Hall encoders accept (check the listing), and skip these. 6 motors × 2 encoder wires = 12 Pi pins; the shifters cover the 5 V case.

items.item: Buck converter 12 V to 5 V, 5 A (for the Pi)
items.note: One 5 A unit covers both the Pi 3 now (needs about 2.5 A, micro-USB) and the Pi 5 later (needs 5 V at up to 5 A over USB-C; the Pi 5 may warn about low current from a simple converter but runs fine). Keep it away from the motor wires.

items.item: Fuse block (6-way blade) + assorted blade fuses (3, 5, 10, 20 A)
items.note: One fuse per rail (see the power plan below): arm 10 A, cart motors 10 A, Pi 3 A (5 A for a Pi 5). The main fuse is the separate 30 A one in the next line.

items.item: Connectors and wire: WAGO lever blocks, JST-XH 4-pin, Dupont jumper wires, 18 AWG and 24 AWG wire
items.note: Thick wire for the 12 V and motor leads, thin for signals. Prices are for one starter kit of each.

items.item: Main fuse: 30 A (MIDI or in-line blade) + holder, and a battery switch
items.note: Fuse right after the battery, then the switch, then the fuse block. Use 12 AWG or thicker (about 3–4 mm²) wire between battery and fuse block; the thin wire in the starter kit is too light for 20 A.

items.item: Heavy wire: 12 AWG (about 4 mm²) red and black, 2 m each, plus ring or spade crimp terminals
items.note: For the battery, fuse, switch and fuse block only. Heavy and bulky for hand luggage, and easy to find in São Paulo (cabo flexível 4 mm², red and black). Estimate, not a quote.

items.item: FINAL battery: 12.8 V 20 Ah LiFePO4 (256 Wh), BMS 30 A or more
items.note: Buy this in São Paulo so it does not have to fly (256 Wh is over the 100 Wh cabin limit, and airlines would stop it). Price is an estimate from memory of typical Mercado Livre listings (about R$ 700–1,100), not a quote; check it. Look for 'LiFePO4' or 'fosfato de ferro', 12.8 V or 12 V, a BMS rated 30 A, and a listing that shows real size: about 180 × 80 × 170 mm, so it will not fit the 70 × 50 × 70 mm CAD battery slot; the cart design needs a bigger battery space, or the battery rides in the unit and a cable goes to the cart. Alternative if cheap: 4 × 32700 LiFePO4 cells with a 4S 30 A BMS board, about R$ 400, but it needs soldering or spot-welding, so not first choice.

items.item: Solar panel: 100 W monocrystalline, for a 12 V system (peak-power voltage about 18 V)
items.note: A rigid 100 W monocrystalline panel for 12 V batteries, about 1.0 × 0.67 m. Estimate R$ 350–550, not a quote. Also try Minha Casa Solar, Neosolar or Aldo Solar for the same size; a 12 V 'nominal' panel with a maximum-power voltage around 18 V suits the controller below. A flexible panel is lighter but costs more and wears out faster.

items.item: Solar charge controller: MPPT 20 A, 12/24 V, with a LiFePO4 setting
items.note: Must have a lithium / LiFePO4 mode that stops at 14.4–14.6 V; a controller set for lead-acid can overcharge or under-charge the battery. A 100 W panel makes only about 8 A at 12.8 V, so 20 A is plenty with room to grow to 200 W. Estimate R$ 250–600 (Epever is a good brand; cheap no-name PWM controllers at about R$ 80 usually have no LiFePO4 setting, so skip them). Not a quote.

items.item: Solar cable 4 mm² with MC4 connectors (5 m) and a 15 A fuse or breaker between panel and controller
items.note: Estimate, not a quote. Order: panel → fuse → controller → battery. Connect the battery to the controller first, the panel last.

items.item: Step-down converter, adjustable, 10 A, set to 12.0 V (for the arm rail)
items.note: A LiFePO4 battery sits at about 13.3 V full and charges to 14.4 V, but the 12 V arm servos and their adapter are only rated to about 12.6 V. This converter sits between the arm's fuse and the Waveshare adapter and holds it at 12 V. Set it with a meter before connecting the arm. The cart motors can take 13–14 V directly. If a 10 A unit is not available, a 12 V 8 A one is fine: the arm is normally well below that.

items.item: Cart omni wheels: printed 38 mm double-row omni wheel (hub halves + rollers)
items.for: Cart: 2 per sleeve (drive wheel and roll wheel), 4 per cart
items.note: Replaces the bought 38 mm omni wheels (about £14 to £19 each, £56 to £76 for four). Print them: files in cad/stl/, print notes in docs/omni-wheel/README.md. Per wheel: 2 hub halves, 14 rollers (print 70 for the cart, 56 plus spares), about 25 g of PETG or ASA. Filament comes from the PLA/PETG line in the Brazil list. Cost is only the filament, about R$ 3 per wheel.

items.item: Omni wheel roller pins: 2 mm steel rod (silver steel or cut nail), cut to 14 mm
items.for: Cart: 14 pins per wheel, 56 per cart
items.note: One 1 m rod gives 70 pins of 14 mm, enough for 4 wheels plus spares. Cut with a hacksaw or a cut-off wheel and file the ends. Stainless 2 mm rod is better outdoors (about £4); carbon steel rusts. Brazil: 'vareta de aço inox 2 mm' or 'barra de aço prata 2 mm', Mercado Livre, about R$ 15.

items.item: Omni wheel screws and nuts: M3 x 14 socket head (stainless) and M3 nuts
items.note: 16 screws and 16 nuts, about £0.15 per pair when bought in a pack of 50 or a small M3 kit (about £7). Brazil: 'parafuso allen M3 x 14 inox' and 'porca M3 inox', Mercado Livre, about R$ 20 for 50. The nuts sit in hex traps in the hub; the heads sit in open recesses.

items.item: Omni wheel grip, variant 1 (picked): O-ring 5 x 1.5 mm, silicone or EPDM
items.for: Cart: 14 rings per wheel, 56 per cart (buy 100)
items.note: 5 mm inside diameter, 1.5 mm thick (written 5 x 1.5, sometimes 5 x 8 outside). A bag of 100 is about £6 to £8. Silicone or EPDM lasts in sun and rain better than the usual black NBR. Brazil: 'o-ring silicone 5 x 1,5 mm' or 'anel o-ring 5x1,5 NBR', Mercado Livre or a local vedações shop, about R$ 25 for 100.

items.item: Omni wheel grip, variant 2 (fallback to test): silicone tube 6 mm inside x 9 mm outside
items.for: Cart: 56 pieces of 7 mm, so 0.4 m, buy 1 m
items.note: Only if the bench test shows the O-rings slip. Buy 1 m of soft food-grade silicone tube, 6 mm inside, 9 mm outside (1.5 mm wall). About £5 to £9. Brazil: 'mangueira de silicone 6 x 9 mm', Mercado Livre, about R$ 20 per metre.

power.title: Power for all twelve motors, in plain words
steps: Who draws what, at 12 V. Arm: six STS3215 servos, each about 0.2 A resting, 0.5–1 A moving a load and up to 2.7 A if jammed (stall). Cart: four 28 mm worm motors, about 0.3–0.5 A when running and 1.5–3 A if jammed (assumed, since the listings do not give it), plus two N20 jaw motors, about 0.2 A running, 0.6 A jammed. Pi: a Pi 3 uses about 2–3 W (0.25 A at 12 V), a Pi 5 about 5–12 W (up to 1 A at 12 V). Those figures are from datasheets and typical listings, not measured here.

Typical use (arm moving and one or two cart motors running): about 3–6 A, which is 40–75 W. Idle, with motors holding position and the Pi on: about 0.7–1 A, about 10 W. Worst case you should plan for (three arm servos pushing hard and two cart motors straining at once): about 15–20 A for a moment. Everything stalled at once would be about 30 A, which should never happen and is what the main fuse is for.

Battery: 12.8 V LiFePO4 (4 cells), 20 Ah (256 Wh) for the final robot, with a protection board (BMS) that allows 30 A continuous. No battery is bought in the UK: it is bought in Brazil, and in the UK the arm runs from a 12 V 5 A bench supply. LiFePO4 is safe and gives a steady 12–13 V. One catch: when full it sits at about 13.3 V and charges to 14.4 V, while the STS3215 servos and the Waveshare adapter are only rated to about 12.6 V. So the arm rail goes through a 12 V step-down converter (in the part list). The cart motors can run on the raw battery voltage.

Fuses: 30 A main fuse right after the battery, then a switch, then a fuse block with three rails. (1) Arm rail, 10 A fuse, then the 12 V step-down converter, then the Waveshare adapter; (2) cart motors rail, 10 A fuse, to the four DRV8871 boards and the jaw board; (3) Pi rail, 3 A fuse (5 A for a Pi 5), to the 5 V converter. Splitting them means a jammed arm servo cannot starve the Pi and make it reboot, and a short on the cart motors blows only its own fuse. Join all grounds at one point.

Pi supply: never power the Pi from the motor rail directly; on the cart use the 5 V, 5 A converter on its own fuse. On the bench in the UK the Pi 3 runs from its own 5.1 V 2.5 A charger (in the part list); if the Pi and the arm adapter share a laptop or USB link, that gives a common ground.

Daily energy budget (rough): about 2 hours a day of real movement at about 60 W is 120 Wh, plus about 22 hours of waiting at about 5 W (Pi, idle servos, converter losses) is 110 Wh, so about 230 Wh a day, call it 250 Wh. The 256 Wh battery then holds about one day with no sun.

Solar for São Paulo: about 4.5 'full-sun hours' a day on average, about 3.5 in winter (typical published figures, tilted to face north). A panel gives about 70% of its label watts after losses. 250 Wh ÷ (3.5 h × 0.7) is about 100 W, so a 100 W panel just covers the budget in winter and has room to spare in summer. If you move more than 2 hours a day, add a second 100 W panel; the controller already allows it.

What to buy where: three groups in the part list. The arm's bench supply, Pi 3 charger and plug adapter in the UK now. The small, light cart parts (motors, wheels, balls, drivers, PCA9685, converters, fuses, connectors, about 1.0 kg) in the UK, carried to Brazil in hand luggage. The battery, solar panel, charge controller, solar cable and heavy wire in Brazil: they are bulky, the battery is lithium and too big for the cabin, and warranty is easier locally. Brazil prices are estimates; check the Mercado Livre pages before paying.

groups.title: UK – for the arm now
groups.blurb: Only what the arm needs to run in the UK. The arm runs from a bench 12 V supply, so no battery is needed. The Pi 3 gets its own small charger.

groups.title: UK – carry to Brazil
groups.blurb: Cart parts that are cheaper in the UK and small and light enough for hand luggage. Nothing lithium, nothing bulky. Order them to your UK address in time: the AliExpress ones take 2–4 weeks.
groups.carry_note: Weight: about 0.94 kg in total (rough, from typical listings; weigh the parcels when they arrive). Awkward in cabin baggage: the motors are small metal gearboxes, so they are dense and show up as dark blobs on the X-ray; pack them in one clear bag, together with the driver boards, so they can be lifted out if asked. The fuse holder, switch and wire kit are fine but can look odd, so keep the receipts. Loose wire spools get tangled, so coil and tape them. Keep it all in one small bag, not in a checked bag, so nothing gets lost. Brazil lets a traveller bring goods up to about US$1,000 by air without import tax, so this is well inside that. Nothing here contains a battery.

groups.title: Buy in Brazil
groups.blurb: Bulky, heavy or lithium items, and workshop items. A cart part from AliExpress shipped straight to Brazil is taxed (about 20% on orders up to US$50 and about 60% above that, plus a state sales tax of about 17–20%, in the 'Remessa Conforme' scheme; check the current rates). That makes it roughly 1.5–2 times the listed price, so the cheap small parts are better bought in the UK and carried.

before_ordering: Links that say 'Search on AliExpress' or 'Amazon UK' are searches, not exact products. Listings come and go, so check each one against the notes before paying.
All prices are estimates, not quotes. The Brazil prices in BRL are from memory of typical Mercado Livre listings: check them.
Rule used: buy in the UK if it is cheaper and light (counting Brazilian import tax on AliExpress orders); buy in Brazil if it is bulky, heavy, lithium, or cheaper there.

CAD mismatch, cart motors: real 28 mm worm motors are often 60–75 mm long, not 55 mm, and the shaft comes out at a right angle. Measure the real motor before changing MOTOR_L or cutting anything. The hinge worm drives are gone in the roll redesign: the four motors are now 2 drives + 2 roll drives.
CAD mismatch, jaw motors: an N20 motor is smaller than the 16 × 30 mm motor in the CAD, so it fits, but the pin mount needs redrawing.
The 20 Ah battery (about 180 × 80 × 170 mm) does not fit the 70 × 50 × 70 mm battery slot in the CAD. The cart needs a bigger battery space, or the battery sits in the unit with a cable to the cart.
No battery is bought in the UK at all. Every battery comes from Brazil.

Omni wheels: the printed 38 mm wheel (docs/omni-wheel/README.md) replaces the bought ones, about £14 to £19 each. One pair of bought 38 mm double aluminium omni wheels (about £18.89 each on Amazon UK) can still be bought as a reference for the bench test (task 290).

Roll redesign (plan task 265): omni wheels are bought in a common 48 or 58 mm size, not the plan's 38 mm, so they are easy to find in both the UK and Brazil. The old hinge worm wheels, worms and hinge pins were never separate lines here, so nothing else is removed.
